title.en: 1. When an elder is the subject: -(으)세요

blocks.h: The honorific rules at a glance
head: What changes
The rule, with examples

blocks.md:
When the **subject of the sentence is someone senior to you** (grandmother, teacher, boss, a customer), you add **-(으)시-** to the verb or adjective to honor that person.

저는 집에 가요. (about me, unchanged)

할머니께서 집에 가**세요**. (about Grandma, honored)

blocks.h: How to build it: check the stem’s batchim
blocks.md:
가**다** → 가 … **no** batchim → attach **-세요** → 가세요

앉**다** → 앉 … **has** a batchim (ㄴ) → attach **-으세요** → 앉으세요

That one check decides everything else. The top two rows of the table above are exactly this rule.

items.tip: Grandma is going home now. / the honorific form of 저는 집에 가요
The boss is coming from the US next week.
The teacher is sitting on the park bench.
Grandpa has been very busy lately.

blocks.md:
**Honoring yourself sounds odd.** -(으)시- is only used when the subject of the sentence is someone senior to you.

저는 지금 가세요. (✕, this honors “me”)

저는 지금 가요. (○)

It’s also not usually used for friends or people your age or younger.

blocks.meaning: Grandma is sitting on the park bench.
blocks.why: The subject is 할머니 (Grandma), someone senior. 앉다 has the batchim ㄴ, so it takes -으세요.

blocks.meaning: The boss is coming from the US next week.
blocks.why: The subject is 사장님 (the boss), and 오다 has no batchim, so -세요 attaches directly.
바쁘다 has no batchim, so -세요 attaches directly to the stem 바쁘.

blocks.q: Which of these can correctly use -(으)세요?
blocks.why: -(으)시- is only used when the subject of the sentence is someone senior to you, not for yourself or a friend.

blocks.q: When talking about someone senior, read -으세요 with a soft, gentle tone.

title.en: 2. Words that change completely, 드시다, 계시다

blocks.md: A handful of words don’t take -(으)시- at all, instead, they **change into a completely different word**. Some are verbs, some are nouns.

items.tip: Grandpa is eating a meal. / the honorific form of 저는 밥을 먹어요
Grandma is sleeping in her room.
Teacher, what is your name? / more polite than 이름이 뭐예요?
Grandma is at home right now.

blocks.md:
**있다 splits into two.** When it means a person “exists,” use **계시다**. When it means “to have” something like time or money, keep the regular -(으)시- and use **있으시다**.

할머니께서 방에 계세요. (○, existence)

선생님, 시간 있으세요? (○: possession)

선생님, 시간 계세요? (✕)

blocks.meaning: Grandpa is sleeping in his room.
blocks.why: The honorific of 자다 changes completely to 주무시다. You don’t just attach -세요 to 자다, as in 자세요.

blocks.meaning: Grandma is in her room right now.
blocks.why: This means a person is present, so it becomes 계시다. 있으세요 is for things you have, like time or objects.
When asking someone senior their name, use 성함 instead of 이름.

blocks.q: 아프다 (honorific) / “할머니, 어디 ___?” (use the honorific of 아프다)
blocks.why: The honorific of 아프다 changes completely to 편찮다, which has the batchim ㅎ, so it takes -으세요.

blocks.q: Match each plain word with its honorific form.

blocks.say: 할머니, 요즘 어떠세요? 진지는 잘 드세요?
blocks.q: These two honorific words often appear together in a greeting.

title.ko: 3강. 같은 문장, 다른 사람: 바꿔 써 보기
title.en: 3. Same sentence, different person, rewrite it

blocks.h: In real use, you rewrite the whole sentence
blocks.md: When you actually speak, first decide **who this is about**, then change **both the verb and the words** to match. Changing only one sounds off.

items.tip: Plain: 집에 가요. / change the subject to 할머니 and attach -세요 to 가다
Plain: 밥을 먹어요. / both 밥→진지 and 먹다→드시다 change
Plain: 나이가 몇 살이에요? / 나이 changes completely to 연세

blocks.md: **Both parts need to change to sound natural.** If you only change the verb, as in “할아버지께서 밥을 드세요,” and leave the noun as is, you get a half-honored sentence. If a word changes completely, change that first.

blocks.meaning: The boss is in the office right now.
blocks.why: This means a person is present, so it becomes 계시다.
When talking about a senior person’s home, use 댁 instead of 집.

blocks.q: Rewrite the basic sentence “집에 가요” as if it’s about your grandmother.
blocks.hint: 가다 has no batchim, so 가 + 세요

blocks.q: Rewrite the basic sentence “밥을 먹어요” as if it’s about your grandfather.
blocks.hint: 밥 becomes 진지, and 먹다 changes completely to 드시다

blocks.say: 할머니, 요즘 어떻게 지내세요? 건강은 괜찮으세요?
blocks.q: This is a phrase people actually use to ask how someone senior is doing.

title.en: Lesson 4. Shaping Honorific Forms by Stem and Batchim

blocks.md:
When honoring someone senior using present polite **-(으)세요**:

- **No 받침:** attach **-세요** (가다 → **가세요**, 보다 → **보세요**).
- **With 받침:** attach **-으세요** (앉다 → **앉으세요**, 읽다 → **읽으세요**).
- **ㄹ stems:** the ㄹ drops completely before ㅅ! (살다 → **사세요**, 만들다 → **만드세요**, 알다 → **아세요**).
- **ㄷ irregular:** ㄷ changes to ㄹ (듣다 → **들으세요**).
- **Special replacement verbs:** use the dedicated honorific word (먹다 → **드세요**, 자다 → **주무세요**).
Never keep the ㄹ in ㄹ verbs when adding -(으)시-! It is **어디 사세요?** (Where do you live?), never *어디 살으세요.

items.tip: Please sit comfortably on the chair. (앉다 + 으세요)
Where do your parents live? (살다 drops ㄹ → 사세요)
Listen carefully to the teacher’s words. (듣다 → 들으세요)

blocks.q: How do you conjugate ‘살다’ (to live) with the honorific ending -(으)세요?
blocks.why: Verbs ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ before ㅅ: 살 + 세요 → **사세요**.

blocks.q: How do you politely tell someone to sit using ‘앉다’?
blocks.why: 앉다 has a final consonant (받침 ㄵ), so it attaches -으세요 → **앉으세요**.

blocks.q: Match each verb with its correct honorific form.

blocks.meaning: Grandmother listens to the radio every morning.
blocks.why: 듣다 changes ㄷ to ㄹ before vowel endings, so it becomes **들으세요**.

blocks.q: Conjugate 만들다 (to make) into the honorific form: 「어머니께서 김치를 ___ .」
blocks.why: The ㄹ drops before ㅅ: 만들 + 세요 → **만드세요**.

blocks.q: Say it out loud politely: “Teacher, please sit in a comfortable seat.”
